summary: Specifies Babel, a loop-avoiding distance-vector routing protocol that works well in both ordinary wired networks and wireless mesh networks. This version obsoletes RFC 6126 and RFC 7557.

plainLanguage.summary: Babel is a way for routers to tell each other how to reach a destination. It works like the older distance-vector protocols, but adds rules that stop packets from being sent round in circles when a link fails, which matters most on shaky wireless links.

questions: what is the babel routing protocol
routing protocol for wireless mesh networks
how does babel avoid routing loops
what is the babel feasibility condition
subtitle: A distance-vector routing protocol built to avoid routing loops in wireless meshes and other changing networks.

tldr.problem: Plain distance-vector routing can send packets round in circles after a network change, and the longer a link takes to notice a failure the worse it gets. Wireless mesh networks make both problems worse.
tldr.mechanism: Babel adds a feasibility condition, so a router only accepts a route it can prove will not create a loop. Each route also carries a sequence number, which lets a starved router ask its source for a fresh one.
tldr.outcome: Babel avoids routing loops in the ordinary case and breaks any loop quickly when a prefix has several sources. It is a Proposed Standard from January 2021 that obsoletes RFC 6126 and RFC 7557 and has not been obsoleted since.

today: RFC 8966 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It obsoletes RFC 6126 and RFC 7557, and it has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: A Routing Protocol for Changing Networks
sections.content:
Babel is a loop-avoiding distance-vector routing protocol designed to be robust and efficient both in networks using prefix-based routing and in networks using flat routing, in other words mesh networks, and both in relatively stable wired networks and in highly dynamic wireless networks. This document describes the Babel routing protocol and obsoletes RFC 6126 and RFC 7557.

The main property that makes Babel suitable for unstable networks is that, unlike naive distance-vector routing protocols such as RIP, it strongly limits the frequency and duration of routing pathologies such as routing loops and black-holes during reconvergence. Even after a mobility event is detected, a Babel network usually remains loop-free. Babel then quickly reconverges to a configuration that preserves the loop-freedom and connectedness of the network, but is not necessarily optimal; in many cases this operation requires no packet exchanges at all. Babel then slowly converges, in a time on the scale of minutes, to an optimal configuration.

More precisely, when every prefix is originated by at most one router, Babel never suffers from routing loops. When a single prefix is originated by multiple routers, Babel may occasionally create a transient routing loop for that particular prefix; the loop disappears in time proportional to the loop's diameter, and the routers involved will not take part in a loop for the same prefix again for an arbitrary garbage-collection time. Assuming bounded packet loss rates, any routing black-holes that appear after a mobility event are corrected in a time at most proportional to the network's diameter.

The RFC also states two limitations. Babel relies on periodic routing table updates rather than a reliable transport, so in large, stable networks it generates more traffic than protocols that only send updates when the topology changes; in such networks OSPF, IS-IS or EIGRP might be more suitable. And unless an optional algorithm is implemented, Babel imposes a hold time when a prefix is retracted, which may make it unsuitable in networks that implement automatic prefix aggregation.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers in a distance-vector protocol each tell their neighbours how far away a destination is, and pick the best offer. The trouble is that when a link dies, the routers can keep pointing at each other for a while. Babel adds rules so that this rarely happens.

sections.title: Why Plain Distance Vector Routing Breaks
sections.content:
Babel is based on the Bellman-Ford algorithm, just like RIP, but includes refinements that either prevent loop formation altogether or ensure that a loop disappears in a timely manner and does not form again. Every node maintains two pieces of data: its estimated distance to a source S, and its next-hop router to S. Periodically each node sends its distance to its neighbours, and a neighbour that receives a smaller total cost switches its next hop and its own distance.

It is well known that a naive application of Bellman-Ford to distributed routing can cause transient loops after a topology change. Consider a source S attached to A, with B and C hanging off A. After convergence, B and C both have a distance of 2 with A as next hop. Suppose the link between S and A fails. When A detects the failure, it switches its next hop to B, which is still advertising a route to S with metric 2, and advertises a metric equal to 3. This process of nodes changing selected neighbours and increasing their metric continues until the advertised metric reaches infinity, a value larger than all the metrics the protocol can carry.
sections.plainLanguage: When a link fails, the routers can end up believing that the route goes through one another, so packets travel in a circle until the numbers grow large enough that everyone gives up. The circle can last long enough to lose real traffic.

sections.title: The Feasibility Condition
sections.content:
Bellman-Ford is robust: its convergence properties survive routers delaying route acquisition or discarding some updates. Babel routers discard received route announcements unless they can prove that accepting them cannot possibly cause a routing loop. The condition that makes this possible is called the feasibility condition, and it turns Bellman-Ford into a family of routing algorithms parameterised by that condition.

One simple feasibility condition, used in DSDV and AODV, accepts an announcement carrying a metric D(B) when the cost from A to B plus D(B) is no larger than A's current distance. If all routers obey this, the metric at every router is nonincreasing, and if A has selected B as its next hop then D(B) is smaller than D(A), which implies the forwarding graph is loop-free.

Babel uses a slightly more refined condition, derived from EIGRP. Given a router A, the feasibility distance of A, written FD(A), is the smallest metric that A has ever advertised for S to any of its neighbours. An update sent by a neighbour B of A is feasible when the metric D(B) advertised by B is strictly smaller than A's feasibility distance, that is when D(B) is less than FD(A). This condition is no more restrictive than the simpler one, and it is strictly less restrictive: in the RFC's example, A has selected the route through B with D(A) equals FD(A) equals 2, and the alternate route through C is feasible for A because D(C) equals 1 is less than FD(A), even though its total cost is 5.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router remembers the smallest number it has ever told its neighbours about a destination. It only accepts a new route if that route claims a smaller number. Since routers only ever advertise numbers that keep shrinking in a chain, the forwarding paths cannot form a circle.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers and Explicit Requests
sections.content:
Feasibility conditions cause starvation when a router runs out of feasible routes. Babel reacts by using sequenced routes, a technique introduced by DSDV and adopted by AODV. In addition to a metric, every route carries a sequence number, a nondecreasing integer that is propagated unchanged through the network and is only ever incremented by the source; a pair of a sequence number and a metric is called a distance. A received update is feasible when either it is more recent than the feasibility distance maintained by the receiving node, or it is equally recent and the metric is strictly smaller.

Instead of waiting for the source to increase its sequence number by itself, Babel lets a node send an explicit request for a new sequence number when it detects that it is suffering from a potentially spurious starvation. The request is forwarded hop by hop to the source with no regard to the feasibility condition. The source then increases its sequence number and broadcasts an update. Because requests ignore the feasibility condition they may be caught in a forwarding loop, which is avoided by having nodes perform duplicate detection for the requests they forward.

When a prefix is originated by several routers, Babel treats routes for the same prefix as distinct entities: every route announcement carries the router-id of its originating router, and feasibility distances are kept per source, where a source is a pair of a router-id and a prefix. Babel therefore guarantees loop-freedom for the forwarding graph to every source, but not in general when a prefix has multiple routers, and any loop will be broken in a time at most proportional to the diameter of the loop.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the safety rule leaves a router with no acceptable route at all. The router then asks the source for a fresh ticket number, which unlocks the route again. When two routers both advertise the same prefix, they are tracked separately, so a loop between them is short-lived rather than permanent.

sections.title: What a Router Keeps and Sends
sections.content:
Every Babel speaker is assigned a router-id, an arbitrary string of 8 octets assumed unique across the routing domain. Babel packets are sent in the body of a UDP datagram, and each packet consists of zero or more TLVs, most of which may contain sub-TLVs. Control traffic can be carried over IPv6 or IPv4, and prefixes of either address family can be announced over either protocol. Using IPv6 exclusively for all control traffic is RECOMMENDED, since using both doubles the traffic devoted to neighbour discovery and link quality estimation.

Each speaker keeps six tables. The interface table lists the interfaces on which it speaks Babel and holds a 16-bit outgoing multicast hello sequence number plus two timers. The neighbour table is indexed by pairs of interface and address, and holds the history of recently received multicast and unicast hellos, the transmission cost from the last IHU, and the hello sequence numbers in both directions. The source table, indexed by prefix, prefix length and router-id, holds the feasibility distances. The route table, indexed by prefix, prefix length and neighbour, holds the routes known to the node, the metric with which each was advertised, its sequence number, the next-hop address and a flag saying whether the route is selected. The table of pending seqno requests lists the requests that have been sent and not yet answered.

Route selection picks a single route per prefix for forwarding and re-advertisement. Two rules are required: a route with infinite metric, that is a retracted route, is never selected, and an unfeasible route is never selected. Beyond that the policy is free, and nodes using different policies will interoperate without creating loops. The obvious policy is to pick the feasible route with the smallest metric, but the RFC recommends adding hysteresis, so that the node only switches away from the current route when the alternative has been consistently good for a while.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router keeps a list of its interfaces, its neighbours, the destinations it knows about, the routes it has learned, and any requests it is still waiting on. It then picks one route per destination to use and to tell its neighbours about.

sections.title: Packets and TLVs
sections.content:
A Babel packet consists of a 4-octet header, followed by a sequence of TLVs forming the packet body, optionally followed by a second sequence of TLVs forming the packet trailer. The header carries a magic value of 42, of which packets with a different first octet MUST be silently ignored; a version field, where this document specifies version 2 and packets with a different second octet MUST be silently ignored; and a body length in octets, excluding the header fields and the trailer. The trailer holds only specialised TLVs that do not need cryptographic protection, and among the TLVs defined here only Pad1 and PadN are allowed there.

With the exception of Pad1, every TLV has a type, a length giving the size of the body in octets exclusive of the type and length fields, and a payload. TLVs with an unknown type value MUST be silently ignored. Sub-TLVs have the same structure and may be carried in the space left over in a self-terminating TLV. The most significant bit of a sub-TLV type is the mandatory bit: sub-TLV types 128 through 255 have it set, and an unknown sub-TLV with the bit set causes the whole enclosing TLV to be ignored, while an unknown sub-TLV without it is simply ignored.

Relative times are carried as 16-bit values counting centiseconds, which allows times up to roughly 11 minutes with a granularity of 10 ms. Addresses have several encodings: a wildcard address of 0 octets, an IPv4 address of 4 octets or less, an IPv6 address of 16 octets or less, and a link-local IPv6 address of 8 octets. A router-id is an arbitrary 8-octet value that must not be all zeroes or all ones.
sections.plainLanguage: A Babel packet starts with four fixed bytes and then a list of self-describing items, each with a type number and a length. Unknown items are skipped rather than treated as an error, which is what lets the protocol be extended later.

sections.title: Registered Numbers
sections.content:
IANA has registered the UDP port number 6696, called "babel", for use by the Babel protocol. It has registered the IPv6 multicast group ff02::1:6 and the IPv4 multicast group 224.0.0.111 for use by the protocol.

Two registries hold the TLV types. In the "Babel TLV Types" registry, the allocation policy is Specification Required for Types 0 to 223 and Experimental Use for Types 224 to 254. The values defined here are Pad1 (0), PadN (1), Acknowledgment Request (2), Acknowledgment (3), Hello (4), IHU (5), Router-Id (6), Next Hop (7), Update (8), Route Request (9) and Seqno Request (10). Types 11 and 12 are the TS/PC and HMAC TLVs defined in RFC 7298, and 13 to 15 are reserved.

The "Babel Sub-TLV Types" registry uses Specification Required for Types 0 to 111 and 128 to 239, and Experimental Use for Types 112 to 126 and 240 to 254. The "Babel Address Encodings" registry defines a wildcard address (0), an IPv4 address (1), an IPv6 address (2) and a link-local IPv6 address (3).
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has a fixed UDP port and two multicast addresses, and each kind of message has a registered number so that other implementations can recognise it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As defined in this document, Babel is a completely insecure protocol. Without additional security mechanisms, Babel trusts any information it receives in plaintext UDP datagrams and acts on it. An attacker on the local network can spoof a Babel packet and redirect traffic by announcing a route with a smaller metric, a larger sequence number or a longer prefix; spoof a malformed packet, which could cause an insufficiently robust implementation to crash; or replay a previously captured packet, which could cause traffic to be redirected or black-holed.

When carried over IPv6, Babel packets are ignored unless they are sent from a link-local IPv6 address, and since routers do not forward link-local IPv6 packets, this mitigates those attacks by restricting them to on-link attackers. No such natural protection exists over IPv4, which is one of the reasons deploying Babel over IPv6 is recommended.

It is usually difficult to ensure that packets arriving at a Babel node are trusted, so it is RECOMMENDED that all Babel traffic be protected by an application-layer cryptographic protocol. Two mechanisms exist: Babel over DTLS, which runs the majority of traffic over DTLS and uses it to authenticate nodes and provide confidentiality and integrity protection, and MAC authentication, which appends a message authentication code to every Babel packet and includes enough extra information to prove the packet is fresh. Both let nodes ignore packets from attackers without the proper credentials. Because MAC authentication is simpler and lighter, it is recommended in preference where its limitations are acceptable, that is where symmetric keying is sufficient and the routing information is not considered confidential. Every implementation of Babel SHOULD implement MAC authentication.

The RFC also notes a privacy concern: the information a mobile Babel node announces to the whole routing domain is sufficient to determine its physical location with reasonable precision, which might cause privacy concerns even if the control traffic is protected. Using randomly chosen router-ids and randomly chosen IP addresses, and changing them often enough, may mitigate this.
sections.plainLanguage: On its own, Babel trusts anyone on the link. An attacker could announce a better route and steal traffic, or replay an old packet. The RFC points at two ways to add protection, one built on DTLS and one that just signs each packet, and notes that a node's own announcements can give away where it is.

fields.name: Magic
fields.desc: The value 42; packets with a different first octet are silently ignored.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Babel protocol version 2; packets with a different second octet are silently ignored.

fields.name: Body Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the body after the header, excluding the trailer.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: The type of the TLV; an unknown type is silently ignored.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the body in octets, exclusive of the Type and Length fields.

fields.name: Payload
fields.desc: The body, which for some TLV types also holds a list of sub-TLVs.

items.label: Acknowledgment Request
items.desc: Asks the receiver to acknowledge the packet.

items.label: Hello
items.desc: The periodic greeting sent to neighbours.

items.label: IHU
items.desc: I Heard You: reports the cost of the link back to the sender.

items.label: Router-Id
items.desc: Carries the router-id used by following Update TLVs.

items.label: Next Hop
items.desc: States the next hop for following Update TLVs.

items.label: Update
items.desc: Advertises a route with its prefix, sequence number and metric.

items.label: Route Request
items.desc: Asks for a route to a prefix.

items.label: Seqno Request
items.desc: Asks the source for a new sequence number.
